calcPage.title: CABLE SIZE CALCULATOR
calcPage.subtitle: Calculate the right cable size for your camper installation.
calcPage.cableLengthHint: One way only — we double it automatically
calcPage.fillFields: Please fill in all fields correctly.
calcPage.step1: Choose Watt or Ampère as input
calcPage.step4: Click Calculate and see your recommendation
calcPage.reason1: Cables that are too thin become dangerously hot
calcPage.seoTitle1: How to calculate the right cable size?
calcPage.seoText1: The right cable size is essential for a safe and efficient 12V or 24V installation in your campervan. A cable that is too thin leads to excessive voltage drop, overheating and in the worst case, fire hazard. By entering the power (Watt) or current (Ampère), cable length and desired maximum voltage drop, our tool calculates the minimum cross-section you need.
calcPage.seoText1b: We use the standard copper conductor formula with a conductivity of 56 m/Ω·mm². The cable length is automatically doubled to account for both the positive and negative conductors. This way you always get reliable advice, whether you're connecting a small fridge or a heavy inverter.
calcPage.seoTitle2: Watt vs. Ampère — what's the difference?
calcPage.seoText2: Watt (W) is the total power consumed by a device, while Ampère (A) is the current flowing through the cable. The relationship is simple: Watt = Volt × Ampère. In a 12V system, a 600W device draws 50A. At 24V it's only 25A — that's why 24V systems are popular at higher powers, as you can use thinner cables.
calcPage.tip1: Always choose the next standard cable size above the calculated minimum — one size larger is safer.
calcPage.tip2: Keep cables as short as possible to limit voltage drop, and bundle positive and negative cables together for a neat installation.
calcPage.tip3: Place a fuse as close to the battery as possible — it protects the cable, not the device.

powerSeo.title1: How to calculate your campervan power consumption?
powerSeo.text1: Daily power consumption in a campervan is measured in watt-hours (Wh). Calculate it by multiplying each appliance's power (in Watts) by the hours you use it per day. For example, a 10W LED light running 4 hours consumes 40Wh per day.
powerSeo.text1b: By adding up all your appliances, you get your total daily consumption. Based on that, you determine the required battery capacity. A LiFePO4 battery offers about 80% usable capacity (e.g. 200Ah × 12.8V × 0.8 = ±2,048Wh), while an AGM battery only provides 50% usable capacity.
powerSeo.title2: LiFePO4 vs AGM — how much capacity do you really need?
powerSeo.text2: A common mistake is comparing LiFePO4 and AGM capacity one-to-one. AGM batteries should only be discharged to 50% to preserve lifespan, while LiFePO4 can be discharged to 80-90%. A 200Ah LiFePO4 battery provides as much usable energy as a 400Ah AGM battery — at half the weight.
powerSeo.tip1: Choose 12V appliances over 230V where possible — an inverter always costs 10-15% energy.
powerSeo.tip2: Solar panels (100-400Wp) can significantly reduce your daily consumption and double your autonomy.
powerSeo.tip3: Monitor your consumption with a battery monitor — this prevents unexpectedly running out of power.

buildSeo.title1: How to choose the right off-grid package?
buildSeo.text1: The ideal energy system depends on three factors: how you use your camper (weekend vs. full-time), which appliances you want to power, and whether you have solar panels. A weekend camper with LED lighting and a phone needs a very different system than a full-timer with a fridge, laptop and coffee maker.
buildSeo.text1b: Our package generator combines these factors and automatically calculates the optimal battery capacity and inverter for your situation. This way you know for sure you're not over- or under-investing.
buildSeo.title2: What's in a complete campervan energy system?
buildSeo.text2: An off-grid energy system for your campervan consists of several components working together:
buildSeo.comp1: LiFePO4 battery (100-300Ah) — the core of your system, stores all energy
buildSeo.comp2: Inverter (1000-3000W) — converts 12V to 230V for household appliances
buildSeo.comp3: Cables (correct thickness!) — connect everything safely, cables that are too thin are a fire hazard
buildSeo.comp4: Fuses & distribution blocks — protect your installation against short circuits
buildSeo.faq1q: Can I upgrade my system later?
buildSeo.faq1a: Yes! LiFePO4 batteries can be connected in parallel. Start with 200Ah and add a second battery later if you need more capacity.
buildSeo.faq2a: Only if you want to use 230V appliances (coffee maker, hair dryer, etc.). Many campervan appliances run directly on 12V, so an inverter isn't always necessary.
buildSeo.faq3q: How long does a LiFePO4 battery last?
buildSeo.faq3a: LiFePO4 batteries last 3,000 to 5,000 charge cycles — that's 8 to 15 years with daily use. By comparison, an AGM battery averages 300-500 cycles.

configurator.installSubtitle: Vehicle-specific installation instructions for your configuration.
configurator.cableSafetyNote: All listed cable sizes are MINIMUM values. When in doubt: always choose one size thicker. A cable that's too thick is never a problem — a cable that's too thin is a fire hazard.
configurator.cableLugWarning: Use welded or crimped cable lugs, NEVER screw terminals.
configurator.tipFuse: ALWAYS place a fuse within 18cm of every positive battery connection.
configurator.tipLabel: Label all your cables with colour or tape — your future self will thank you.
configurator.tipTest: Test the entire system BEFORE you put the panels back.
configurator.tipPhotos: Take photos of every step — invaluable for troubleshooting later.
configurator.safetyFuseDesc: ALWAYS place a fuse within 18cm of every positive battery connection. Every positive cable leaving the battery MUST be fused. This is your protection against short circuits and fire.
configurator.safety230vDesc: A 230V installation in a metal vehicle is life-threatening without proper grounding and an RCD/RCCB (30mA). ALWAYS have the 230V installation inspected by a certified electrician.
configurator.safetyFrostDesc: LiFePO4 batteries must NOT be charged at temperatures below 0°C. This causes permanent damage (lithium plating). Use a battery with built-in heating or disable all charging sources in freezing temperatures.
configurator.safetyCableDesc: Use only tinned copper marine cable or automotive-grade cable (min. 105°C insulation). NEVER use cheap hardware store cable. Use crimped cable lugs with a hydraulic crimping tool. NEVER solder heavy cables (>10mm²).
configurator.safetyWeightDesc: After installing batteries, converter, solar panels, furniture, water tank, etc., your vehicle may exceed the maximum allowed weight (GVW). This is unsafe AND illegal. Check the total weight at a weighbridge after conversion. A LiFePO4 battery is ~50% lighter than an AGM of the same capacity — choose LiFePO4 to save weight.
configurator.phase0Step1: Gather all your components and verify everything is complete. Lay everything out on a clean workspace.
configurator.phase0Step2: Read this entire guide FIRST before you start. Understand the order.
configurator.phase0Step3: Disconnect the negative terminal of your starter battery. This prevents short circuits during installation. The starter battery is located at: {{location}}.
configurator.phase0Step4: Take photos of the current state of your van — you'll want to compare later.
configurator.phase0Step5: Ensure you have all tools (see list below). Missing something? Buy it now, not halfway through the install.
configurator.phase0Step6: Plan where each component will go. Sketch it on paper or mark positions with tape. Measure everything.
configurator.phase0Warning: NEVER work on an electrical installation alone. Always have someone nearby for emergencies.
configurator.phase1Step1: Check that your {{ah}}Ah LiFePO4 battery fits in the recommended location (see card above).
configurator.phase1Step2: Build or buy a sturdy mounting bracket. The battery MUST be firmly secured — it must not shift during emergency braking or an accident.
configurator.phase1Step3: Place the battery and secure it. Ensure the terminals remain accessible.
configurator.phase1Step4: Do NOT connect the battery yet. We'll do that in Phase 4.
configurator.phase1Step5: Mount the ANL main fuse ({{fuseSize}}A) + fuse holder and the battery disconnect switch directly next to the battery positive terminal. Order: Battery + → ANL fuse (within 18cm!) → Disconnect switch → rest of system.
configurator.phase1Step6: Mount the negative busbar near the battery.
configurator.phase1Warning: The battery should be placed as low and central as possible for optimal centre of gravity. Ensure at least 2cm clearance around it for air circulation.
configurator.phase2Step1: Choose a central, accessible location for the fuse box. Ideal: near the battery, dry spot, accessible for maintenance.
configurator.phase2Step2: Mount the fuse box securely to a wall or panel.
configurator.phase2Step3: Mount the negative busbar near the fuse box (if not already at the battery).
configurator.phase2Step4: Label the fuse box now with a permanent marker: which circuit goes in which slot (lighting, fridge, USB, water pump, etc.).
configurator.phase2Step5: Insert the correct fuses in each slot (lighting: 5A, USB: 5A, fridge: 10A, water pump: 5A, diesel heater: 10A, roof vent: 5A). Don't connect yet.
configurator.phase3Intro: This is the most time-consuming phase. Route all main cables BEFORE connecting anything.
configurator.phase3Warning: Check EVERY pass-through for sharp edges. File down metal edges and use rubber grommets. A cable rubbing against a sharp metal edge = short circuit = fire.
configurator.route1Step1: Your vehicle's starter battery is located at: {{location}}.
configurator.route1Step2: Run a positive cable ({{size}}mm², red) AND a negative cable (same size, black) from the starter battery to the DC-DC charger location.
configurator.route1Step4: Distance: approximately {{distance}}m. Buy cables at least 50cm longer than the measured distance.
configurator.route1Step5: Protect the cable with {{protection}} along the entire length.
configurator.routeDoNotConnect: Do NOT connect anything yet — only route and cut the cable with 10cm excess on each end.
configurator.route2Step1: Short route (usually <1 metre). Keep the cables as short as possible.
configurator.route3Step1: Run a {{size}}mm² positive cable from the battery disconnect switch to the fuse box.
configurator.route3Step2: Run a {{size}}mm² negative cable from the negative busbar to the fuse box.
configurator.route4Step1: The inverter must be as CLOSE to the battery as possible. Max 1.5 metre cable length.
configurator.route4Step2: Use {{size}}mm² cable — this is the thickest cable in your system.
configurator.route4Step4: This cable needs a separate ANL fuse, sized to the cable.
configurator.route4HeavyCableWarning: For inverters >2000W: consider double cable sets in parallel. ALWAYS use crimped cable lugs with a hydraulic crimping tool.
configurator.route5Step1: The cable enters the roof via a waterproof roof gland.
configurator.route5Step2: Drill a hole in the FLAT part of the roof (not on a rib/reinforcement). Use a step drill.
configurator.route5Step3: Mount the waterproof roof gland and seal with Dekalin or Sikaflex.
configurator.route5Step4: Run the MC4 cable from the solar panel through the gland inside.
configurator.route6Step1: Short cable from MPPT output to the battery. Use {{size}}mm² cable.
configurator.cableTip1: Label EVERY cable on BOTH ends with tape + marker.
configurator.cableTip2: Use split loom or cable trunking to protect cables from chafing.
configurator.cableTip3: Tie cables down with cable ties every 30-50cm. No loose cables.
configurator.cableTip5: Take photos of every route before putting trim panels back.
configurator.phase4OrderWarning: IMPORTANT: Connect in THIS order. Work from the consumers BACK to the battery. The battery is the LAST thing you connect.
configurator.phase4Step1Desc: Connect your 12V appliances to the correct position in the fuse box. Positive wire to the fused output, negative wire to the negative busbar.
configurator.phase4Step2a: Connect the battery cables to the MPPT FIRST (output side).
configurator.phase4Step2b: THEN connect the solar panel cables to the MPPT (input side).
configurator.phase4Step2c: NEVER the other way around! The MPPT must 'see' a battery before you connect the panels.
configurator.phase4Step3a: Connect the thick cables to the inverter: red to +, black to -.
configurator.phase4Step3b: Use crimped cable lugs. Tighten the bolts firmly.
configurator.phase4Step3c: Do NOT connect the 230V output yourself unless you're a qualified electrician.
configurator.phase4Step4a: Connect the starter battery cables to the INPUT of the DC-DC charger.
configurator.phase4Step4b: Connect the leisure battery cables to the OUTPUT of the DC-DC charger.
configurator.phase4Step4c: Connect the Remote On/Off signal (ignition-switched 12V) so the DC-DC only charges when the engine is running.
configurator.phase4Step5a: Check EVERYTHING one more time. Trace every cable. Check every connection.
configurator.phase4Step5b: Use a multimeter to check for short circuits: resistance between positive and negative should be infinite (OL).
configurator.phase4Step5c: Connect the NEGATIVE cable to the battery FIRST.
configurator.phase4Step5d: THEN connect the positive cable to the ANL fuse.
configurator.phase4Step5e: If all is well: no sparks, no sounds, no heat.
configurator.phase4Step5f: Turn the battery disconnect switch ON.
configurator.phase4SparkWarning: If there's a spark or pop when connecting: STOP IMMEDIATELY. Disconnect and find the short circuit.
configurator.phase5Step1: Turn the battery disconnect switch ON.
configurator.phase5Step2: Measure the battery voltage with a multimeter: should be between 12.8V and 13.6V for a full LiFePO4.
configurator.phase5Step3: Test each consumer individually: lighting, fridge, USB ports, water pump.
configurator.phase5Step4: Test the inverter: turn it on, connect a small 230V device (e.g. phone charger). Measure output: should be stable 230V.
configurator.phase5Step5: Test the solar panel: check the MPPT display/app — does it show input voltage? In sunlight: is charge current flowing?
configurator.phase5Step6: Test the DC-DC charger: reconnect the starter battery, start the engine, check if the DC-DC is charging.
configurator.phase5Step7: Let the system run for 30 minutes and check ALL connections for heat. NOTHING should be warm. Heat = bad connection = danger.
configurator.phase5Warning: Perform these tests BEFORE you put trim panels/furniture back. You need access to every cable and connection in case something's wrong.
configurator.phase6Step1: Check that all cables are neatly secured and protected.
configurator.phase6Step2: Take photos of the complete installation — every connection, every route, every component.
configurator.phase6Step3: Create a wiring diagram or print the one from this guide and keep it in the van.
configurator.phase6Step4: Note at the fuse box which circuit is in which position.
configurator.phase6Step5: Place a sticker at the battery disconnect switch: 'EMERGENCY SWITCH — in case of fire or fault: turn OFF'.
configurator.phase6Step6: Store spare fuses in the van (near the fuse box).
configurator.phase6Step7: If you have a 230V system: have it INSPECTED by a certified electrician before use.
configurator.phase6Step8: Only now put the seat, trim panels and furniture back.
configurator.phase6Step9: Test all functions again after reassembly.

configurator.otherSmartAltQuestion: DOES YOUR VEHICLE HAVE A SMART ALTERNATOR?
configurator.otherSmartAltHint: This determines which charging solution you need.
configurator.otherSmartAltHelpText:
Measure the voltage on your starter battery with a multimeter while the engine is running:

• Constant 13.8-14.4V → Conventional alternator
• Fluctuating voltage (12.5-14.8V) → Smart alternator
• Voltage drops to ~12.5V when warm → Smart alternator

Not sure? Choose 'smart alternator' — you'll always be safe.
configurator.otherVoltageHint: Most cars and vans are 12V. Trucks are often 24V.
configurator.other24vWarning: ⚠️ VanXcel products only work on 12V. For a 24V system you need a 24V→12V converter before the VanXcel system.
